repo.name: synctang
repo.description: Personal F-Droid repository publishing signed synctang releases, built automatically in CI from commits and tags. synctang unlocks a LUKS volume at boot by asking a human's phone, which holds its key in the Android Keystore and never discloses it.

application.name: synctang key holder
application.summary: Approve a Linux machine's disk unlock without ever holding its passphrase.
application.desc:
synctang unlocks a LUKS-encrypted Linux machine while it is still sitting at its boot prompt, with a person in the loop for every single unlock.
This app is the key holder. What makes it different from a remote-passphrase app is what it does not have: it never holds the machine's disk passphrase, or anything from which the passphrase could be worked out. It holds one long-term key, generated inside the phone's secure hardware and unable to leave it. The machine sends a blinded challenge point; the phone does one elliptic curve agreement against that point and sends back the result; the machine, and only the machine, turns that into the key that opens the disk.
The protocol is McCallum-Relyea key agreement, the same idea behind Tang and Clevis, with the key holder's half moved into a phone's Keystore and put behind a biometric. A recording of the whole exchange tells an eavesdropper nothing, and answering a challenge tells the phone nothing about the disk.
How it works:
- Pair once by scanning the QR code the machine shows, and enrol this phone's public key on the machine. - When the machine boots, it waits at its prompt and asks. The phone shows the machine's cryptographically verified identity, and the name it gave itself. - One Unlock button, behind a strong biometric. The key is created so that the phone's secure hardware, not this app, refuses to use it without a recent biometric match. - Optionally, the machine can print a code on its own console that has to be checked on the phone first, so that somebody who has only stolen the disk cannot get an unlock approved over the network.
Machine and phone find each other over the public Syncthing relay network, so no port forwarding and no server of your own are needed. The relay sees two identities and some traffic; the tunnel inside it is TLS 1.3 pinned to those identities, so the relay operator cannot read or alter the exchange.
Deliberately not supported: unattended reboots. If a machine has to come back up on its own, use Tang directly. This project trades that away for a human approval and a key that lives in hardware.
No tracking, no analytics, no proprietary libraries. Free software under the GNU Affero General Public Licence, version 3 or later.
